title: Staying in shape in camp; Germans young and old
summary: The daily orchestra rehearsals kept his chops fit, and Briggs jokes about the signature muted-trumpet note, and distinguishes decent older guards from young Hitler Youth recruits.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Right. Well, how did you get out after the war when you picked up playing again?
Well, you see, in the camp, as we had this orchestra, we rehearsed everyday. That was a good thing.
So your chops were in pretty good shape.
Oh, yes, they were in pretty good shape for playing what you call light music, and things like that.

When I came out, I have to get myself in shape again, for resistance and everything, you see, endurance. Yes, I managed to keep up pretty nicely. But in our camp we used to have wonderful fun, 'cause at the end of our concerts, I would play with the -- with a muted trumpet. And, as soon as I hit the first note, all the internees would come to attention (?). (Laughter). So the Gerries said, "What are you playing?" I said, "It's our signature tune, it's the end of the concert. That's all there is." He said, "You're sure." I said, "Sure, they're all getting up because they're thanking us for the concert we just played." (Laughter). You know, it wasn't that. MR. COLLIER: Sure. MR. BRIGGS: You know, we had -- some of the Germans of a certain age, were

pretty congenial. We had -- also, some of those were youngsters that I'll never forget, from -- more or less, either from Holland, or from Denmark. Kids, fifteen years old. They tried to boot you and everything else.
Oh, yes. Kids, fifteen years old. Yeh, we avoided them, we stayed away from them.
Yes, they were tough, what they would call "the Hitler youngsters", you see.
